status_reasoning: Multiple independent lines of evidence converge on this conclusion: localization of plus-end (UNC-104) and minus-end (KLP-16, DHC-1) motors, dynamic MT imaging with EBP-2, phenotypes in three independent alleles, and cell-autonomous rescue. The specificity to dendrites (no axonal defects) strengthens the conclusion.

While EM data clearly shows MT bundling with visible cross-bridges in the presence of kinesin-1 and NudC, the requirement for NudC (a cofactor not mentioned in vivo) raises questions about physiological relevance. The in vitro conditions may not fully recapitulate the in vivo mechanism, and direct evidence of antiparallel MT cross-linking in neurons is lacking.

Structure-function analysis with UNC-116MT (C-terminal MT-binding mutant) shows differential rescue of cargo transport versus MT polarity, demonstrating both domains are required. The increased MT density in mutant dendrites (C71-C75) supports the sliding-out model rather than sliding-in. Multiple alleles affecting different domains show consistent phenotypes.

Multiple protein markers show predicted mislocalization patterns: axonal proteins (RAB-3, SYD-2) ectopically accumulate in dendrites while dendritic proteins (ACR-2, CAM-1, FBN-1) fail to accumulate. This demonstrates that MT polarity is instructive for neuronal compartmentalization, though quantification is provided for only some markers.

Clear genetic separation of kinesin-1 functions: klc-2 mutants phenocopy unc-116 for mitochondrial transport but show no MT polarity defects, even in klc-1;klc-2 double mutants. This is consistent with prior work showing KLC-independent MT gliding in Drosophila S2 cells, supporting a conserved mechanism.

UNC-116MT rescues dendrite length but not MT polarity, demonstrating these are separable phenotypes. The observation that dendrite outgrowth direction and timing are normal in unc-116 mutants indicates MT polarity is not required for initial dendrite formation, only for maintenance of proper length and protein compartmentalization.

Two independent measures (GFP::TBA-1 intensity ratio and EBP-2::GFP comet frequency) both show increased MT density in unc-116 mutant dendrites. This supports the model that kinesin-1 slides plus-end-out MTs out of dendrites rather than sliding minus-end-out MTs in, though the magnitude of the effect could be better quantified with statistical analysis.

TOM-20 localization defects in unc-116 mutants and rescue by UNC-116MT demonstrate the canonical cargo transport function is intact in the C-terminal MT-binding mutant. This validates the mutant as a tool to separate transport from polarity functions and confirms kinesin-1's established role in mitochondrial transport.
